title.justification: This title directly reflects the focus of the paper, which explores the relationship between loneliness and changes in neurocognition with aging.
title.quote: How to cite this article: Spreng RN, Bzdok D. Loneliness and Neurocognitive Aging. Adv Geriatr Med Res. 2021;3(2):e210009.

analysis.description: This paper discusses the impacts of loneliness on neurocognitive aging, particularly in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic. It explores how loneliness may alter brain structure and function, notably affecting the 'default mode network', and suggests public health strategies to mitigate loneliness among older adults.

type.justification: The paper primarily discusses hypotheses and theoretical links between loneliness and neurocognitive changes without presenting new empirical data or experiments.
type.quote: Yet uncertainty surrounds the precise biological mechanisms which link loneliness in humans to normative brain aging and neurodegenerative disease.

name.justification: The paper investigates the neural impacts of loneliness, focusing particularly on brain structure and function, which falls under the neuroscience domain.
name.quote: We have identified the default network as a core substrate of perceived social isolation and loneliness in the human brain.

name.justification: The paper focuses on older adults and the aging process, particularly in relation to brain health and loneliness.
name.quote: Loneliness imposes significant risks to physical, mental and brain health in older adulthood.

name.justification: The paper discusses social isolation and loneliness in relation to brain networks, specifically the default mode network associated with social cognition.
name.quote: ...we describe how the experience of loneliness may alter the structure and function of the human brain.

name.justification: The paper references the UK Biobank as a data resource used to study loneliness and brain health.
name.quote: Drawing from the UK Biobank, the most comprehensive biomedical dataset, we examined loneliness, brain volume, functional connectivity and structural connectivity in approximately 40,000 middle to older age adults.
